Description: ask patient necessary ice-breaking questions (such as what's the purpose of visit or any necessary question to make patient feel comfortable and build connections; these are not related to the symptoms and it is only for ice-breaking) to initiate the interview. the criteria is met when the patient has depressed mood
Patient_Story: I decided to visit the psychiatrist because I felt an overwhelming sense of sadness lately. I remember sitting in the waiting room, staring at the floor, thinking about how I hadn't really felt happy in months, especially after losing my job last year. I was hoping that maybe talking to someone could help me make sense of all these heavy feelings weighing me down.

Description: the patient has reported clinicallly significant manic or hypomanic symptoms
Patient_Story: Lately, I’ve been having these intense bursts of energy that feel almost out of control. Just last week, I couldn’t sit still during dinner with my friends at a local restaurant; I kept jumping from topic to topic, and at one point, I even suggested we go skydiving on a whim! I felt invincible, but now I wonder if that was just a manic episode, especially since I haven’t been sleeping much at all.

Description: criteria met for a manic episode (i.e., **at least 1 week of elevated**, expansive or irritable mood accompanied by increased activity or energy and other characteristic symptoms sufficiently severe to cause marked impairment). Duration has to be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: For the past week, I've been riding this incredible wave of energy. Just two days ago, I went for a run at the park and ended up running twice as far as I usually do, feeling as if I could conquer anything. My friends have noticed too; they mentioned I seem “wired” and even a bit too talkative during our video calls. It’s exhilarating, but there's a nagging feeling inside me that makes me question whether this is all too much.

Description: The patient meets the criteria if they acknowledge having a history of delusions or hallucinations.
Patient_Story: During that same high-energy week, one night alone in my apartment I thought I saw shadows moving along the walls and heard whispers I couldn't make out. It only happened while I was in that state; once the high passed, it stopped.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient's psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during manic or major depressive episodes.
Patient_Story: During my recent manic episode, I experienced some really troubling psychotic symptoms. One night, while I was out with friends, I suddenly believed that I could communicate with the stars, thinking they were giving me special messages about my future. This was incredibly vivid, and I remember feeling a mix of excitement and confusion as I shared my revelations with everyone around me. It was only later, when I returned to a more stable state, that I realized those thoughts were not based in reality and were part of the manic phase I was going through.

The criteria are met if the patient has experienced one or more major depressive episodes without any history of manic or hypomanic episodes. To determine if a major depressive episode has occurred, the following aspects must be examined:
1. Interest or pleasure in doing things
2. Sleeping conditions
3. Energy level
4. Appetite
5. Feelings of self-worth
6. Concentration when doing things
7. Changes in movement or speech
8. Suicidal ideation
9. Duration of at least 2 weeks
The decision should be based on an overall assessment of the severity of these aspects, considering the patient's responses across all areas (not all aspects need to be abnormal). The duration of symptoms should be explicitly asked and confirmed as lasting at least 2 weeks before making a final decision. Be really caucious when making the decision!
